# How to use this file

**Lab 10 starter.** Work through the handout (Lab10.pdf) in this file. Each section has a code chunk with hints and `Your answer` lines to complete. The data are typed in for you (8 rows from the handout).

* Base R only. Run chunk by chunk or **Knit**. There is **no data file to download**: the 8 rows of the table in the handout are entered in the first chunk.
* The handout gives a few **check values** in each table (for example Table 1, bP = 111.5 and 121.5). Reproduce them first, then fill in the blanks.
* Your parameter estimates will be **close to, but not exactly equal to**, the handout values ($\beta_{ref}$ = -6.107, $\beta_{bP}$ = 0.0245): the handout values are rounded and
  were obtained with another program. Small differences in the 2nd or 3rd decimal of the expected values are normal.

## The key relationships (read before starting)

Each row of the data is a group of $N$ men with blood pressure $bP$. Among them, $N_{hd}$ developed heart disease. The response variable is a **proportion**.

| Quantity | Formula | In words |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Morbidity | $p = N_{hd} / N$ | proportion of men with heart disease |
| Odds | $odds = p / (1 - p)$ | heart disease cases per non-case (1-p) |
| Odds ratio | $OR = odds / odds_{ref}$ | odds relative to the reference category (bP = 111.5) |
| Linear predictor | $\eta = \beta_{ref} + \beta_{bP}\, bP$ | the model: $\eta = \log(odds)$ |
| Expected odds | $E(odds) = e^{\eta}$ | back-transform the linear predictor |
| Expected odds ratio | $E(OR) = e^{\beta_{bP}\,\Delta bP}$ | $\Delta bP$ = bP minus the reference bP (111.5) |
| Expected morbidity | $E(p) = E(odds) / (1 + E(odds))$ | back from odds to a proportion |

(1) The linear predictor ($\eta$) is a straight-line equation ($y = a + bx$), except instead of predicting the proportion of heart disease directly, it predicts the odds of heart disease for a given blood pressure on log scale log-odds ($\log(odds)$) for a given blood pressure.

(2) $\beta_{ref}$ is the baseline log-odds at the reference blood pressure, and $\beta_{bP}$ is the slope, which is how much the log-odds change for every $1$-unit increase in blood pressure.

The data are from Cornfield (1962), reported by Agresti (1990): $N$ = number of men aged 40 to 59 in the Framingham study, $N_{hd}$ = number who developed heart disease.

\newpage

# The data

```{r data}
Cornfield <- data.frame(
  bP  = c(111.5, 121.5, 131.5, 141.5, 151.5, 161.5, 176.5, 191.5),   # blood pressure (mmHg)
  N   = c(156, 252, 284, 271, 139, 85, 99, 43),                      # sample size (men)
  Nhd = c(3, 17, 12, 16, 12, 8, 16, 8))                              # men who developed heart disease
Cornfield
str(Cornfield)
```

# Section 1. Preliminary calculations: observed morbidity, odds and odds ratios

Calculate the morbidity, the odds and the odds ratio for every blood pressure level. The reference category is bP = 111.5, so its odds ratio is 1 by definition.
The handout shows the first two rows and the odds ratio at 151.5 (4.819) as checks.

**Table 1.** Fill in all the blank cells. Someone explain the computation? 

```{r t1}
# (1) Morbidity: proportion of men with heart disease
Cornfield$Morb = Cornfield$Nhd / Cornfield$N
Cornfield$Morb
#### (2) Odds = p / (1 - p)
Cornfield$Odds <- Cornfield$Morb / (1 - Cornfield$Morb)
#### (3) Odds ratio relative to the reference category (the first row, bP = 111.5)
Cornfield$OR <- Cornfield$Odds / Cornfield$Odds[1]
Table1 <- Cornfield[, c("bP", "N", "Nhd", "Morb", "Odds", "OR")]
round(Table1, 3)
```

# Section 2. Model definition

The model for the change in odds of heart disease with blood pressure is

$$Odds = e^{\eta} + \textit{binomial error}, \qquad \eta = \beta_{ref} + \beta_{bP}\, bP$$
Replacing the terms we have,

$$Odds = e^{\beta_{ref} + \beta_{bP}\, bP} + \textit{binomial error}$$


Response: the proportion $N_{hd}/N$ of men who developed heart disease (binomial counts out of $N$ men)

Explanatory variable: blood pressure bP (continuous, mmHg)

Error: binomial

```{r normal_vs_binomial}
set.seed(42)

# Set up side-by-side plots and save original graphics settings
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 3.5, 1.5))

# ==========================================================
# 1. NUMERIC (CONTINUOUS) VARIABLE -> NORMAL ERROR
# ==========================================================
x_num  <- seq(30, 75, length.out = 60)
mu_num <- 95 + 0.75 * x_num                  # Linear expected value E(Y)
sigma  <- 8                                  # Constant error standard deviation
y_num  <- rnorm(length(x_num), mean = mu_num, sd = sigma)

plot(x_num, y_num,
     pch = 16, col = rgb(0.2, 0.4, 0.7, 0.7),
     ylim = c(95, 175),
     xlab = "Predictor (e.g., Age in years)",
     ylab = "Numeric response (e.g., Blood pressure)",
     main = "Numeric Variable\n(Normal Error)")

lines(x_num, mu_num, col = "black", lwd = 2)
lines(x_num, mu_num + 1.96 * sigma, col = "firebrick", lty = 2, lwd = 1.5)
lines(x_num, mu_num - 1.96 * sigma, col = "firebrick", lty = 2, lwd = 1.5)

legend("topleft",
       legend = c("Observed Y", "Expected E(Y)", "95% Normal range (constant)"),
       pch = c(16, NA, NA), lty = c(NA, 1, 2), lwd = c(NA, 2, 1.5),
       col = c(rgb(0.2, 0.4, 0.7, 0.7), "black", "firebrick"),
       bty = "n", cex = 0.8)

# ==========================================================
# 2. PROPORTION VARIABLE (p = N_hd / N) -> BINOMIAL ERROR
# ==========================================================
bP   <- seq(105, 185, length.out = 60)
N    <- 20                                   # Men per blood pressure group
eta  <- -14.5 + 0.10 * bP                    # Linear predictor (log-odds)
E_p  <- exp(eta) / (1 + exp(eta))            # Expected morbidity E(p)
N_hd <- rbinom(length(bP), size = N, prob = E_p)
p_obs <- N_hd / N                            # Observed proportion

# Smooth grid for expected curve and 95% binomial prediction interval
bP_grid  <- seq(105, 185, length.out = 200)
eta_grid <- -14.5 + 0.10 * bP_grid
p_grid   <- exp(eta_grid) / (1 + exp(eta_grid))
low_bin  <- qbinom(0.025, size = N, prob = p_grid) / N
high_bin <- qbinom(0.975, size = N, prob = p_grid) / N

plot(bP, p_obs,
     pch = 16, col = rgb(0.1, 0.6, 0.4, 0.7),
     ylim = c(-0.05, 1.12),
     xlab = "Blood pressure (bP)",
     ylab = "Proportion response (p = N_hd / N)",
     main = "Proportion Variable\n(Binomial Error, N = 20)")

abline(h = c(0, 1), col = "gray60", lty = 3) # Hard bounds at 0 and 1
lines(bP_grid, p_grid, col = "black", lwd = 2)
lines(bP_grid, high_bin, col = "firebrick", lty = 2, lwd = 1.5)
lines(bP_grid, low_bin, col = "firebrick", lty = 2, lwd = 1.5)

legend("topleft",
       legend = c("Observed p = N_hd / N", "Expected morbidity E(p)", "95% Binomial range (varies)"),
       pch = c(16, NA, NA), lty = c(NA, 1, 2), lwd = c(NA, 2, 1.5),
       col = c(rgb(0.1, 0.6, 0.4, 0.7), "black", "firebrick"),
       bty = "n", cex = 0.8)

# Restore original graphics parameters
par(op)
```

Describe the model in words:

> **Your answer:** \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

The observed odds of developing heart disease is the expected odds $e^{\eta}$ + plus random binomial error $\textit{binomial error}$. The expected odds change exponentially with blood pressure.

# Section 3. Model execution

Fit the logistic regression with `glm()`: binomial error, logit link, response entered as the proportion `Nhd / N` with the number of trials `N` as **weights**.
(Equivalent alternative: `cbind(Nhd, N - Nhd) ~ bP`, giving the numbers of successes and failures.)

```{r fit}
HdModel <- glm(Nhd / N ~ bP, family = binomial(link = logit), weights = N, data = Cornfield)
summary(HdModel)

# Parameter estimates: beta_ref (intercept) and beta_bP (slope on the log-odds scale)
beta_ref <- unname(coef(HdModel)[1])
beta_bP  <- unname(coef(HdModel)[2])
round(c(beta_ref = beta_ref, beta_bP = beta_bP), 4)

# Same model with the successes / failures form of the response (check: identical estimates)
#HdModel_b <- glm(cbind(Nhd, N - Nhd) ~ bP, family = binomial, data = Cornfield)
#all.equal(coef(HdModel), coef(HdModel_b))
```


Report the Parameter estimates:

> **Your answer:** 
$\hat\beta_{ref} = -6.082$
$\hat\beta_{bP} = 0.0243$

**Interpretation of the parameters.** 

(1) The intercept is the predicted log-odds of heart disease when the predictor variable equals $0$
At $bP = 0\text{ mmHg}$, $\eta = -6.082$ BUT $\eta$ is on the log-scale

On the odds scale:$E(\text{odds}) = e^{-6.082} \approx 0.0023$ cases per non-case.

(2) The slope tells us how the risk of heart disease changes with blood pressure

On the log-scale: Every $+1\text{ mmHg}$ increase in blood pressure adds $0.0243$ to the linear predictor $\eta$. $\beta_{bP} > 0$, thus, higher blood pressure increases heart disease risk

On the odds scale: the slope turns addition into a constant multiplier:$$e^{0.02434} \approx 1.0246$$

Each $+1\text{ mmHg}$ increase in blood pressure multiplies the expected odds of heart disease by $1.0246$, that is $2.46\%$ increase in odds per mmHg.

*Using the model for prediction*

Calculate the odds of heart disease at bP = 111.5 mmHg. 

```{r interp1}
exp(beta_ref)                      # e^beta_ref: the odds when bP = 0 (an extrapolation, far outside the data)
exp(beta_ref + beta_bP * 111.5)    # the odds at bP = 111.5 mmHg (uses both parameters)
```


*The model predicts $0.0344$ men developing heart disease for every $1$ man who does not, in other words, $3.44$ men develop heart disease for every $100$ men* 

Calculate the rate of change in the odds per unit change in blood pressure, $e^{\beta_{bP}}$, in %/mmHg.

```{r interp2}
exp(beta_bP)                       # exp(slope) factor by which the odds are multiplied per +1 mmHg
100 * (exp(beta_bP) - 1)           # per cent change in the odds per mmHg
# The formula comes directly from combining the multiplicative property of exponents with the standard definition of percent change.
```


A percent change of $2.4637\%$ per mmHg means that for every $+1\text{ mmHg}$ increase in blood pressure, a man's expected odds of developing heart disease increase by about $2.46\%$ 

# Section 4. More calculations: expected odds ratios, expected odds and expected proportions

## Table 2: expected odds ratio (the ratio of two odds)

$\Delta bP$ is the blood pressure minus the reference (111.5). The expected odds ratio is $E(OR) = e^{\beta_{bP}\,\Delta bP}$.

```{r t2}
Cornfield$bP
Cornfield$bP[1]
# Change the NA_real_ into the blood pressure minus the reference BP (111.5) 
Table2 = data.frame(bP = Cornfield$bP, dbP = NA_real_)   # change in bP from the reference
Table2$E_OR = exp(beta_bP * Table2$dbP)                                           # E(OR) = exp(beta_bP * dbP)
round(Table2, 3)
```

## Table 3: expected odds

Using both parameter estimates, calculate the expected odds at each observed blood pressure level

Use both parameters: $\eta = \beta_{ref} + \beta_{bP}\, bP$ and $E(odds) = e^{\eta}$. 

We calculate: (1) slope x BP (2) linear predictor and (3) expected odds from estimated parameters (refer to the table in prelimary for details)

```{r t3}
Cornfield$bP
# Change beta_ref to the correct value
Table3 <- data.frame(bP = Cornfield$bP, beta_ref = beta_ref, beta_bP = beta_bP)
Table3
Table3$beta_bP_x_bP = beta_bP * Table3$bP          # beta_bP * bP slope x BP
Table3
Table3$eta = Table3$beta_ref + Table3$beta_bP_x_bP   # linear predictor
Table3
Table3$E_Odds = exp(Table3$eta)               # expected odds
round(Table3, 3)
```

**Prediction at an unobserved value.** Calculate the expected odds ratio and the expected odds at bP = 181.5 mmHg (not in the data).

```{r pred181}
# Hints: same formulas as Tables 2 and 3, with bP = 181.5
# Change 0 to get the correct answer
bP_new <- 181.5
c(E_OR   = exp(beta_bP * (0 - 111.5)),         # expected odds ratio relative to 111.5
  E_Odds = exp(beta_ref + beta_bP * bP_new))   # expected odds at 181.5
```

## Table 4: expected morbidity

The formula to calculate the expected morbidity from odds is $$p = odds / (1 + odds)$$ 

```{r t4}
# Hints: E(Morb) = E(Odds) / (1 + E(Odds))
Table4 = data.frame(bP = Cornfield$bP, Obs_Morb = Cornfield$Morb)
Table4$E_Morb = Table3$E_Odds / (1 + Table3$E_Odds)       # p = odds / (1 + odds)
round(Table4, 3)
```

# Section 5. Model evaluation

As in the general linear model, we check homogeneity and normality of the residuals.

But with logistic regression we use **deviance residuals**.

Plot the deviance residuals against the fitted proportions and make a normal scores plot. Label the points with the observation numbers (1 to 8).

```{r diag, fig.width=7, fig.height=3.8, fig.cap="Lab 10: deviance residuals vs fitted proportions (left) and normal scores (right)."}
dres  <- residuals(HdModel, type = "deviance")     # deviance residuals extracted
fit_p <- fitted(HdModel)                           # fitted proportions extracted

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
# Left: deviance residuals against the fitted proportions
plot(fit_p, dres, xlab = "fitted proportion", ylab = "deviance residuals",
     main = "Deviance residuals vs fits", xlim = c(0.02, 0.22), ylim = c(-1.5, 2.2))
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
text(fit_p, dres, labels = 1:8, pos = 4)           # observation numbers

# Right: normal scores plot of the deviance residuals
q <- qqnorm(dres, main = "Normal scores", ylim = c(-1.5, 2.2))
qqline(dres)
text(q$x, q$y, labels = 1:8, pos = 3)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

round(dres, 2)
```

The first, second, and third observations deviate from the line, due primarily to the second
observation.

Observation 2 (bP = 121.5) has the largest deviance and is the outlier in both plots

observations 1 and 3 deviate mainly because of it. Its observed morbidity (0.067) is much higher than the expected 0.042: given the model, too many men had heart disease at 121.5 mmHg. 
The other residuals are small and the normal scores plot is otherwise close to the line.

## Removing the outlier and refitting

Set up a new data table **without** the bP = 121.5 row, refit the model, and report the new parameter estimates. Then calculate the expected odds ratio and the expected odds at bP = 191.5
with the new estimates.

```{r refit}
Cornfield2 <- Cornfield[-2, c("bP", "N", "Nhd")]      # remove row 2 (bP = 121.5)
# Define a new model without observation 2
HdModel2 <- glm(Nhd / N ~ bP, family = binomial(link = logit), weights = N, data = Cornfield2)
summary(HdModel2)

beta2_ref <- unname(coef(HdModel2)[1])
beta2_bP  <- unname(coef(HdModel2)[2])
round(c(beta_ref = beta2_ref, beta_bP = beta2_bP), 4)

# Expected odds ratio, odds and morbidity at bP = 191.5 with the new estimates
bP_x <- 191.5
E_OR2 <- exp(beta2_bP * (bP_x - 111.5))
E_Odds2 <- exp(beta2_ref + beta2_bP * bP_x)
c(E_OR = E_OR2, E_Odds = E_Odds2, E_Morb = E_Odds2 / (1 + E_Odds2))
```

$\hat\beta_{bP}$ = 1$

### Generalization

State the direction of change in the expected morbidity, expected odds and expected odds ratio at **any** level of bP when the regression parameter $\beta_{bP}$ increases or decreases.
Check your generalization against several values of bP: this table compares the values before and after at every observed bP.

```{r q3}
chk <- data.frame(bP = Cornfield$bP)
chk$OR_before <- exp(beta_bP  * (chk$bP - 111.5))
chk$OR_after <- exp(beta2_bP * (chk$bP - 111.5))
chk$Odds_before <- exp(beta_ref  + beta_bP  * chk$bP)
chk$Odds_after <- exp(beta2_ref + beta2_bP * chk$bP)
chk$Morb_before <- chk$Odds_before / (1 + chk$Odds_before)
chk$Morb_after <- chk$Odds_after  / (1 + chk$Odds_after)
round(chk, 3)

# The blood pressure at which the two fitted log-odds lines cross
(beta2_ref - beta_ref) / (beta_bP - beta2_bP)
```

> **Answer:** 
**Expected odds ratio:** $E(OR) = e^{\beta_{bP}\,\Delta bP}$ depends only on $\beta_{bP}$. 
For every bP above the reference ($\Delta bP > 0$) it **increases** when $\beta_{bP}$ increases and **decreases** when $\beta_{bP}$ decreases (at the reference it is always 1).

The table shows OR_after > OR_before at every bP > 111.5. 

**Expected odds and morbidity:** they depend on both parameters ($\beta_{ref}$ and $\beta_{bp}$) through $\eta = \beta_{ref} + \beta_{bP}\, bP$. If $\beta_{ref}$ is fixed, a larger $\beta_{bP}$ raises $\eta$, hence the odds and the morbidity, at every bP > 0 (morbidity moves with the odds because $p = odds/(1+odds)$ is increasing). 


```{r q4, fig.width=10, fig.height=3.8}
# Grid of blood pressures and the two fitted curves (before = all 8 points, after = without bP = 121.5)
bP_seq <- seq(105, 195, by = 0.5)
eta_before <- beta_ref  + beta_bP  * bP_seq                 # log-odds, before
eta_after  <- beta2_ref + beta2_bP * bP_seq                 # log-odds, after
OR_before  <- exp(beta_bP  * (bP_seq - 111.5))           # expected odds ratio (reference 111.5)
OR_after   <- exp(beta2_bP * (bP_seq - 111.5))
p_before   <- 1 / (1 + exp(-eta_before))              # expected morbidity = odds / (1 + odds)
p_after    <- 1 / (1 + exp(-eta_after))

cross <- (beta2_ref - beta_ref) / (beta_bP - beta2_bP)            # bP where the two log-odds lines cross
col_b <- "black"; col_a <- "blue"                     # before = black solid, after = blue dashed
pt_col <- ifelse(Cornfield$bP == 121.5, "red", "grey40")   # observation 2 (bP = 121.5) in red

par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 3, 1))

# Panel A: log-odds scale: two straight lines that pivot around a crossing point
plot(bP_seq, eta_before, type = "l", lwd = 2, col = col_b, ylim = c(-4.2, -1),
     xlab = "blood pressure (mmHg)", ylab = "log-odds  (eta)", main = "A. Log-odds: the line pivots")
lines(bP_seq, eta_after, lwd = 2, lty = 2, col = col_a)
points(Cornfield$bP, log(Cornfield$Odds), pch = 16, col = pt_col)   # observed log-odds
abline(v = cross, lty = 3)
text(cross, -4.1, paste0("cross at ", round(cross)), pos = 4, cex = 0.8)
legend("topleft", legend = c("all 8 points", "without bP = 121.5", "obs. 2 (121.5)"),
       lty = c(1, 2, NA), pch = c(NA, NA, 16), col = c(col_b, col_a, "red"), lwd = c(2, 2, NA), bty = "n", cex = 0.8)

# Panel B: odds ratio scale: depends on the slope only, so 'after' is above 'before' beyond the reference
plot(bP_seq, OR_before, type = "l", lwd = 2, col = col_b, ylim = c(0, 15),
     xlab = "blood pressure (mmHg)", ylab = "odds ratio vs 111.5", main = "B. Odds ratio: slope only")
lines(bP_seq, OR_after, lwd = 2, lty = 2, col = col_a)
points(Cornfield$bP, Cornfield$OR, pch = 16, col = pt_col)           # observed odds ratios
abline(h = 1, lty = 3)

# Panel C: morbidity scale: S-shaped curves that cross (same crossing point as panel A)
plot(bP_seq, p_before, type = "l", lwd = 2, col = col_b, ylim = c(0, 0.25),
     xlab = "blood pressure (mmHg)", ylab = "morbidity", main = "C. Morbidity: curves cross")
lines(bP_seq, p_after, lwd = 2, lty = 2, col = col_a)
points(Cornfield$bP, Cornfield$Morb, pch = 16, col = pt_col)          # observed morbidity
abline(v = cross, lty = 3)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

Panel A: a larger slope with a lower intercept means the line is lower below 168 and higher above it.
Panel B: the odds ratio depends only on the slope, so it is higher everywhere past the reference.
Panel C: morbidity follows the same crossing as the log-odds

## Extra: the formula for a proportion from the odds

Starting from $odds = p/(1-p)$, use algebra to obtain $p = odds/(1 + odds)$.

> **Answer.** $odds = \dfrac{p}{1-p} \;\Rightarrow\; odds\,(1-p) = p \;\Rightarrow\; odds - odds\cdot p = p \;\Rightarrow\; odds = p + odds\cdot p = p\,(1 + odds) \;\Rightarrow\; p = \dfrac{odds}{1 + odds}.$
